tips: Keep your chin tucked towards your chest to maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement.
Focus on driving through your heels to maximize glute activation.
Control the eccentric (lowering) phase to enhance muscle growth.
Use a pad or towel under the dumbbell for comfort.

name: Dumbbell Pistol Squat
desc: The Dumbbell Pistol Squat is an advanced single-leg squat variation that builds significant lower body strength, balance, and mobility, primarily targeting the quadriceps and glutes.
steps: Stand tall, holding a dumbbell in each hand with your arms hanging at your sides.
Lift one leg straight out in front of you, keeping it extended throughout the movement.
Lower your body by bending the knee of your standing leg, keeping your chest up and back straight.
Descend until your glutes are close to your heel or your thigh is parallel to the floor, maintaining balance.
Push through your heel to return to the starting position, extending your standing leg fully.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs and repeat for the other side per set.
tips: Start with bodyweight pistol squats to master the movement pattern before adding dumbbells.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down at your sides and keep your chest up to stay balanced over the working foot.
Focus on controlling the eccentric (lowering) phase to improve stability and strength.
Elevate your heel slightly on a small plate if ankle mobility is a limiting factor.

name: Dumbbell Push Press
desc: A compound overhead press that uses a leg drive to initiate momentum and develop shoulder and triceps power.
steps: Stand holding dumbbells at shoulder height with palms facing forward.
Slightly bend your knees into a quarter squat.
Drive through your legs to generate momentum, then press the dumbbells overhead.
Lock out your arms at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder height with control.
tips: Use a shallow dip — this is not a full squat.
Drive the heels into the floor to initiate the press.
Keep your core braced to protect the lower back.

name: Dumbbell Reverse Fly
desc: A hinged isolation exercise raising dumbbells out to the sides, targeting the rear deltoids and upper back.
steps: Hinge forward at the hips holding dumbbells with arms hanging down.
Keep your back flat and knees slightly bent.
Raise the dumbbells out to the sides until level with your shoulders.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back with control.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Use a light weight so the rear delts do the work, not momentum.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Keep a soft, fixed bend in your elbows throughout.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
desc: A hip-hinge movement with dumbbells and soft knees, loading the hamstrings and glutes through a controlled stretch.
steps: Stand holding dumbbells in front of your thighs with a soft knee bend.
Hinge at the hips and push your glutes back.
Lower the dumbbells along your legs until you feel a hamstring stretch.
Keep your back flat and shoulders pulled back.
Drive your hips forward to return to standing.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Keep your knee angle constant; the movement is a hinge, not a squat.
Tuck your chin slightly to keep your spine in one straight line.
Squeeze your glutes at the top without leaning backward.

name: Dumbbell Side Bend
desc: A standing oblique isolation exercise using a dumbbell to develop lateral core strength and stability.
steps: Stand upright holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side.
Keep the opposite hand on your hip or behind your head.
Bend laterally toward the dumbbell side, lowering it along your thigh.
Return to upright, then bend to the opposite side using only your obliques.
Complete all reps per side.
tips: Avoid leaning forward or backward — move strictly sideways.
Use a controlled tempo in both directions.
Keep the weight close to your leg throughout.

name: Dumbbell Snatch
desc: An explosive single-arm lift driving a dumbbell from the floor to overhead in one fluid motion.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, dumbbell on the floor between your feet.
Hinge and grip the dumbbell with one hand.
Explosively extend hips, knees, and ankles to pull the dumbbell upward.
Punch the dumbbell overhead in one fluid motion.
Lock out your arm and stabilize at the top.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
tips: Extend your hips and knees fully before pulling with your arm.
Punch the dumbbell up to a stable overhead lockout.
Keep the dumbbell close to your body as it rises.

name: Dumbbell Split Squat
desc: A split-stance squat holding dumbbells at the sides, training the quads and glutes one leg at a time.
steps: Stand in a split stance holding dumbbells at your sides.
Keep your torso upright and core braced.
Lower your back knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Stop when your front thigh is parallel to the floor.
Drive through your front heel to return to standing.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
tips: Keep most of your weight on your front leg.
Lower your back knee straight down toward the floor.
Track your front knee over your toes without letting it cave inward.

name: Dumbbell Tricep Extension
desc: A single-arm overhead tricep extension for balanced arm development.
steps: Stand holding a dumbbell in one hand overhead.
Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending your elbow.
Extend your arm back to the starting position.
Keep your elbow close to your head.
Repeat on both sides.
tips: Move only your forearm, keeping the upper arm still.
Brace your core to avoid arching your lower back.
Choose a weight light enough to reach a full stretch.

name: Dumbbell Upright Row
desc: A compound pulling movement with dumbbells that targets the lateral deltoids and upper trapezius.
steps: Stand holding two dumbbells in front of your thighs, palms facing your body.
Pull the dumbbells straight up along your body, leading with your elbows.
Raise until the dumbbells reach chin height and elbows are above the wrists.
Pause briefly, then lower with control.
Repeat for the desired reps.
tips: Keep the dumbbells close to your body throughout.
Lead with your elbows, not your hands.
Avoid pulling with a very narrow grip to reduce shoulder impingement risk.

name: Dumbbell Windmill
desc: This full-body exercise builds core stability, shoulder strength, and hip mobility by rotating the torso while holding a dumbbell overhead, primarily targeting the obliques and lateral deltoids.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell overhead in one hand, arm locked.
Turn your feet slightly away from the dumbbell side, keeping the arm straight and eyes on the weight.
Hinge at your hips, pushing them out to the side of the dumbbell, and slowly lower your torso towards the floor.
Keep your back straight and the dumbbell arm vertical as you reach your free hand towards your foot or the floor.
Reverse the motion by driving through your hips and obliques to return to the starting position.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch and repeat for the other side.
tips: Maintain a tight core throughout the movement to protect your spine and enhance stability.
Keep your eyes fixed on the dumbbell overhead to help maintain balance and a straight arm.
Focus on hinging at the hips, not rounding your back, to engage the hamstrings and glutes.
Start with a light weight to master the form before progressing to heavier loads.

name: Dumbbell Wrist Curl
desc: A dumbbell wrist curl that isolates the forearm flexors and trains both arms independently.
steps: Sit on a bench with the forearm resting on the thigh, palm up.
Hold a dumbbell with the wrist hanging off the knee.
Let the dumbbell roll down to the fingertips.
Curl the dumbbell up by flexing the wrist.
Lower under control. Complete reps per side.
tips: Move only at the wrist — keep the forearm still.
Roll the dumbbell to the fingertips for full range.
Train both arms with the same load and reps.

name: Eagle Pose
desc: A standing balance with one leg wrapped over the other and the arms twined in front of the chest, holding a narrow, compact shape on a single bent leg.
steps: Stand tall, bend both knees slightly and shift the weight onto one foot.
Cross the other thigh over the standing thigh and hook the foot behind the calf if it reaches.
Cross the opposite arm underneath, wind the forearms and bring the palms towards each other.
Sit down a little into the standing leg and hold for the prescribed time with the elbows lifted.
Unwind and repeat on the other side.
tips: Let the crossed foot rest on a block or the floor if hooking it behind the calf is not available.
Lift the elbows to shoulder height to keep the upper back working rather than collapsing.
Sink lower on the standing leg only while the knee tracks over the middle of the foot.

name: Easy Pose
desc: A simple cross-legged seat used for breathing and meditation: the pelvis stays upright, the spine is tall and the hips settle without strain.
steps: Sit on the floor and cross the shins comfortably, each foot under the opposite knee.
Sit up on a folded blanket or cushion until the knees rest below the level of the hips.
Stack the ribs over the pelvis and let the hands rest on the thighs.
Hold the seat for the prescribed time, breathing slowly and evenly.
Switch which shin is in front on the next round so both sides get equal time.
tips: If the knees float high, raise the seat rather than forcing them down.
Let the chin stay level so the neck follows the line of the spine.
Support the knees on cushions when a long sit gets uncomfortable.

name: Elliptical Trainer
desc: A low-impact cardio machine movement in which the feet trace a continuous oval on the foot plates while the moving handles push and pull, working the legs and upper body together.
steps: Step onto the foot plates one at a time, holding the fixed centre post until you are steady, then take a moving handle in each hand.
Start the pedals turning forward, keeping your whole foot down on the plate rather than lifting your heel.
Push one handle away as the opposite foot travels forward, and pull the other back, so the arms and legs work in opposition.
Stand tall with your hips over the pedals and your core braced instead of hanging back on the handles.
Set the resistance and ramp so you can hold a smooth stride, and continue for the desired time or distance.
tips: Drive the handles rather than letting the legs push them for you — the arm work is most of what makes the elliptical a full-body machine.
Keep your heels down on the plates. Riding on the toes cramps the calves and cuts the glutes out of the stride.
Pedalling backwards for part of the session shifts the emphasis toward the hamstrings and glutes and breaks up a long steady effort.

name: Extended Side Angle Pose
desc: A wide-stance standing pose with the front knee bent and the torso extended over the front thigh, so one long line runs from the back heel to the top hand.
steps: Stand wide with the front foot turned out and the back foot angled slightly in.
Bend the front knee until it stacks over the ankle and keep the back leg straight.
Rest the front forearm on the thigh, or the hand on the floor or a block, and reach the top arm over the ear.
Hold the position for the prescribed time, turning the chest towards the ceiling.
Straighten the front leg to come up and repeat on the other side.
tips: Press the outer edge of the back foot down; the pose loses its base as soon as that heel lifts.
Keep the front knee pointing at the middle toes rather than drifting inwards.
Take the forearm on the thigh instead of the hand on the floor to keep the chest open.

name: EZ-Bar Bench Press
desc: A flat-bench chest press performed with an EZ bar, whose angled grips are easier on the wrists while still loading the pectorals, front delts, and triceps.
steps: Lie flat on a bench with your feet planted on the floor, gripping the EZ bar's angled bends over your chest.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your lower chest with your arms extended.
Lower the bar under control toward your lower chest.
Press the bar back up to full arm extension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Keep your feet flat on the floor and maintain a slight arch in your lower back for a stable base.
The EZ bar's angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight barbell.
Lower the bar to your lower chest and keep your elbows tucked at roughly 45 degrees to protect the shoulders.

name: EZ-Bar Curl
desc: An isolation exercise targeting the biceps using an EZ-bar, which reduces wrist strain compared to a straight barbell.
steps: Stand holding an EZ-bar with an underhand grip on the angled portions.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping your elbows pinned.
Squeeze at the top, then lower under control.
Repeat.
tips: Use the inner or outer grip to vary emphasis.
Keep your wrists neutral on the angled grips.

name: EZ-Bar Front Raise
desc: A two-handed front raise with an EZ-bar. The angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar while still letting both hands drive the same load.
steps: Stand holding an EZ-bar with an overhand grip on the inner bends, arms hanging in front of the thighs.
Keep the elbows slightly bent and fixed throughout.
Raise the bar in a smooth arc up to shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower under control.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: Raise and lower the bar along the same smooth arc, without swinging it away from the body.
Do not swing the torso; keep the core braced and the knees slightly soft.
Stop at shoulder height — going higher shifts tension off the front delts.

name: EZ-Bar Lying Triceps Extension
desc: A lying triceps extension performed with an EZ bar to isolate the triceps through a full range of motion.
steps: Lie on a flat bench holding an EZ bar over your chest with a narrow grip.
Lower the bar toward your forehead by bending at the elbows.
Extend your arms back to the start.
Repeat.
tips: Keep your upper arms vertical throughout so the triceps do the work.
The EZ bar's angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar.
Lower slowly to protect the elbows.

name: EZ-Bar Overhead Tricep Extension
desc: Overhead tricep extension with an EZ-bar — the angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar while keeping the long head under a deep stretch.
steps: Stand or sit holding an EZ-bar overhead with an overhand grip on the inner bends.
Arms fully extended, bar above the head.
Bend only the elbows to lower the bar behind the head in an arc.
Keep the upper arms vertical and close to the head; only the forearms move.
Extend the elbows to return the bar overhead.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: If the elbows flare out, drop the load — flared elbows mean shoulders are assisting.
The deeper the stretch at the bottom, the better the long-head hypertrophy stimulus.
A seated version is easier on the lower back.

name: EZ Bar Pullover
desc: This compound exercise targets the lats and pectorals by extending the arms overhead with an EZ bar, promoting upper body strength and hypertrophy.
steps: Lie supine on a flat bench with your head slightly off the end, holding an EZ bar with a pronated grip.
Extend the bar straight above your chest, keeping a slight bend in your elbows.
Slowly lower the bar in an arc behind your head, feeling a stretch in your lats and chest.
Pull the bar back to the starting position using your lats and pectorals.
Maintain control throughout the movement, avoiding momentum.
tips: Keep your core braced to prevent arching your lower back excessively.
Focus on a deep stretch at the bottom of the movement.
Use a spotter for heavier loads to ensure safety.
Control the eccentric (lowering) phase for maximum muscle engagement.

name: EZ-Bar Reverse Curl
desc: A reverse curl with an EZ-bar targeting the brachialis and forearm extensors with a comfortable grip.
steps: Hold an EZ-bar with an overhand grip.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Lower under control.
Repeat.
tips: Keep elbows close to your torso.
The EZ-bar reduces wrist strain.

name: EZ Bar Reverse Grip Row
desc: This compound pulling exercise targets the latissimus dorsi and biceps, effectively building back thickness and arm strength with an underhand grip.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding an EZ bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Hinge at your hips, keeping a slight bend in your knees and your back straight, until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor.
Let the bar hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.
Pull the bar towards your lower abdomen, squeezing your shoulder blades together and driving your elbows up.
Control the eccentric phase, slowly lowering the bar back to the starting position with full arm extension.
tips: Maintain a neutral spine throughout the movement to protect your lower back.
Focus on initiating the pull with your lats, not just your biceps.
Avoid shrugging your shoulders; keep them depressed and retracted.
Use a full range of motion, extending your arms completely at the bottom.

name: EZ-Bar Romanian Deadlift
desc: A Romanian deadlift using an EZ-bar. The angled grip is easier on the wrists and suits lighter hinge work or elbow-sensitive lifters.
steps: Stand holding an EZ-bar at mid-thigh with an overhand grip on the inner bends.
Feet hip-width, soft bend in the knees, chest up, lats engaged.
Push the hips back while letting the bar slide down the front of the legs.
Go until you feel a deep hamstring stretch without rounding the lower back.
Drive the hips forward to return to standing, keeping the bar close to the body.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: The movement is a hip hinge, not a squat — knees barely bend.
The EZ-bar is shorter than a barbell; grip the inner bends for a neutral-ish wrist.
Stop at the bottom of your clean ROM — no round-back stretch.

name: EZ-Bar Shrug
desc: A shrug using an EZ-bar for a comfortable grip while loading the trapezius.
steps: Stand holding an EZ-bar in front of you.
Shrug your shoulders straight up.
Hold at the top, then lower.
Repeat.
tips: Avoid rolling the shoulders in circles.
Use a full range of motion.

name: EZ Bar Spider Curl
desc: A chest-supported curl over an incline bench with an EZ bar, isolating the biceps with strict form.
steps: Lie chest down on an incline bench holding an EZ bar with underhand grip.
Let your arms hang straight down from your shoulders.
Curl the bar up toward your shoulders.
Squeeze your biceps at the top of the movement.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Let your arms hang straight down and keep the upper arms fixed.
Curl with the biceps only — the bench removes any excuse to swing.
Lower to a full stretch before starting the next rep.

name: EZ-Bar Upright Row
desc: An upright row variation using an EZ-bar for more comfortable wrist positioning.
steps: Stand holding an EZ-bar with a shoulder-width grip on the angled portions.
Pull the bar straight up along your body toward your chin.
Lead with your elbows, keeping them above your hands.
Lower with control.
Repeat.
tips: Pull only as high as your shoulders allow without pinching.
Keep the bar close to your body throughout the movement.
Avoid swinging or using your legs to lift the weight.

name: EZ-Bar Wrist Curl
desc: A wrist curl with the EZ-bar, friendlier on the wrists than a straight bar.
steps: Sit on a bench with forearms resting on the thighs, palms up.
Grip an EZ-bar on the inner bends with hands shoulder-width.
Let the bar roll down to the fingertips.
Curl the bar up by flexing the wrists.
Lower under control.
tips: The EZ-bar's angle is gentler on the wrists than a straight bar.
Move only at the wrist — keep the forearms still.
Roll the bar to the fingertips for full range.

name: Fire Hydrant
desc: A bodyweight glute exercise performed on hands and knees: one knee is lifted out to the side, like a dog at a fire hydrant, while the hips and spine stay square to the floor. It targets the gluteus medius and the other hip abductors with no equipment.
steps: Set up on hands and knees with the hands under the shoulders, the knees under the hips and the back flat.
Brace the trunk so the hips stay level and square to the floor.
Keeping the knee bent at about 90 degrees, lift one knee out to the side until the thigh is roughly parallel to the floor.
Pause briefly at the top without rotating the pelvis or leaning away from the working side.
Lower the knee back to the starting position under control.
Complete the repetitions on one side, then switch legs.
tips: Move only at the hip; if the lower back twists or the torso tips, the range is too big.
Keep the knee bent at the same angle for the whole set.
Press the supporting hand and knee into the floor so the standing side does not sag.

name: Fish Pose
desc: A supine backbend supported on the forearms with the chest lifted and the head tilted back, opening the front of the chest and the throat.
steps: Lie on your back with the legs straight and the arms alongside the body, palms down under the hips.
Press the forearms into the floor and lift the chest towards the ceiling.
Let the crown of the head rest lightly on the floor without putting weight through the neck.
Hold the position for the prescribed time, breathing into the upper chest.
Lift the head, then lower the back down.
tips: Carry the weight in the forearms, not the head; the neck only guides the position.
Place a block lengthwise under the upper back if the floor version pinches.
Keep the legs active and the thighs rolling slightly inwards.

name: Flexed Arm Hang
desc: A static pull-up hold in which the chin is kept above a bar with the elbows bent. It builds endurance and strength in the arms, lats and grip and is a classic stepping stone to the pull-up.
steps: Grip a pull-up bar with the palms facing away, a little wider than shoulder-width, or facing you for an easier version.
Pull yourself up, or step up on a box, until the chin is above the bar.
Keep the elbows bent and pointing down, with the shoulders pulled away from the ears.
Hold the position without swinging, keeping the legs together and the trunk tight.
Lower slowly to a full hang when the chin begins to drop.
tips: Keep the chin clearly above the bar; once it drops below, the hold is over.
Squeeze the bar and pull the shoulder blades down and back.
Step up to the top position rather than jumping if you cannot yet pull up.

name: Floor EZ-Bar Press
desc: A floor press variation using an EZ-bar for a more comfortable wrist and elbow position.
steps: Lie on the floor holding an EZ-bar over your chest.
Lower the bar until your elbows touch the floor.
Press back up to full extension.
Repeat.
tips: The EZ-bar reduces wrist strain vs. a straight bar.
Keep your feet flat on the floor.

name: Floor Kettlebell Pullover
desc: A pullover done lying on the floor with a kettlebell held by the handle or by the horns. The floor limits the range of motion compared to the bench version, which reduces shoulder strain and makes it a good home-gym or prehab option.
steps: Lie face-up on the floor with knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a kettlebell by the handle with both hands above your chest, arms almost straight (slight elbow bend).
Keeping the elbow angle fixed, lower the bell overhead in an arc until the upper arms touch the floor.
Pull the bell back above the chest along the same arc.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: The floor caps the ROM; if it feels too short, use a bench version.
Grip the handle firmly and squeeze the lats at the top.
Keep the lower back flat against the floor throughout.

name: Floor Press
desc: A barbell pressing movement performed on the floor, limiting range of motion and taking the lower body out of the equation.
steps: Lie on the floor and position yourself under a barbell in a rack.
Unrack the bar and lower it to your chest until your upper arms touch the floor.
Press back up to lockout.
Repeat.
tips: Elbows touching the floor provides a natural stopping point.
Useful for addressing lockout weakness.

name: Flutter Kicks
desc: A supine core drill alternating small up-and-down leg kicks while the lower back stays pressed to the floor.
steps: Lie flat on your back with your legs extended.
Place your hands under your glutes for support.
Lift both legs a few inches off the floor.
Alternate kicking your legs up and down in a small range.
Keep your core braced and lower back pressed down.
Continue for the desired duration or reps.
tips: Press your lower back into the floor for the whole set.
Keep the kicks small and steady rather than big and wild.
Raise your legs higher if you feel your lower back arching.

name: Frog Stretch
desc: A floor stretch for the inner thighs and groin: on your hands and knees, you slide the knees wide apart with the feet turned out and rock your hips back toward your heels. The wide knees open the adductors while the hips stay low.
steps: Start on your hands and knees on the floor, with your wrists under your shoulders.
Slide your knees out to the sides as far as is comfortable and turn your feet out, keeping your shins in line with your knees.
Lower onto your forearms and keep your back straight, not rounded.
Rock your hips back toward your heels until you feel a strong stretch along your inner thighs.
Hold the position and breathe slowly, keeping your hips level.
Come out by sliding the knees together and sitting back before you stand.
tips: Put a folded towel or mat under your knees if the floor is hard.
Go only as wide as you can keep your hips level; letting the pelvis tilt takes the stretch out of the inner thighs.
Rock back slowly and ease out of the position if you feel any pinching at the front of the hips.

name: Front Lever
desc: An advanced static hold under the bar with the body horizontal and chest facing upward, requiring straight-arm pulling strength through the lats and core.
steps: Grip the bar with an overhand grip and hang.
Tuck your knees to your chest and pull your straight arms down toward your hips, leaning back until your torso is horizontal and your chest faces up.
Extend your body horizontally with arms straight and chest facing the ceiling.
Keep your body rigid and parallel to the floor.
Hold for the desired duration, then tuck and lower under control.
tips: Progress through tuck and straddle holds before attempting the full extension.
Squeeze your core and glutes to prevent the hips from dropping.
Keep the shoulders actively depressed away from the ears throughout the hold.

name: Garland Pose
desc: A deep bodyweight squat held with the heels down and the elbows pressing the knees open, used to open the hips, ankles and lower back.
steps: Stand with the feet a little wider than the hips and the toes turned slightly out.
Squat down as low as the ankles allow, keeping the heels on the floor.
Bring the palms together at the chest and press the elbows against the inner knees.
Hold the position for the prescribed time with the chest lifted and the spine long.
Press through the feet to stand back up.
tips: Roll a towel under the heels if they lift; forcing them down rounds the lower back instead.
Widen the stance to make room for the pelvis rather than squeezing into a narrow squat.
Press the knees and elbows against each other lightly to keep the chest from collapsing.

name: Glute Bridge
desc: A bodyweight glute activation exercise performed lying on the floor.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Drive your hips up by squeezing your glutes.
Hold briefly at the top with hips fully extended.
Lower your hips back down with control.
Repeat.
tips: Push through your heels rather than your toes.
Avoid arching your lower back at the top.
Don't let your knees cave inward as you lift.

name: Glute Bridge Hold
desc: The top of the glute bridge held for time: hips fully extended with the shoulders, hips and knees in one line, so the glutes stay under tension instead of cycling through reps.
steps: Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat, about hip-width apart and close enough to brush your fingertips with your heels.
Push through the heels and lift the hips until the body forms a straight line from the knees to the shoulders.
Squeeze the glutes and tuck the ribs down so the lower back does not take over.
Hold the top position for the prescribed time, keeping the weight in the heels.
Lower the hips under control to finish the set.
tips: Push the knees slightly outwards during the hold to keep the glutes engaged.
Stop lifting once the knees, hips and shoulders form a straight line; going higher usually means arching the back.
For extra load, rest a dumbbell or a plate across the hips before the lift.

name: Glute Kickback
desc: A bodyweight glute isolation exercise performed on all fours to develop gluteus maximus strength and shape.
steps: Begin on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Keeping the knee bent at 90 degrees, drive one heel toward the ceiling.
Squeeze the glute at the top of the movement.
Lower the leg back to the starting position with control.
Complete all reps, then switch sides.
tips: Keep your hips square to the floor — avoid rotating.
Focus on squeezing the glute, not just lifting the leg.
Add a resistance band or cable for progressive overload.

name: Glute Kickback Hold
desc: The end position of the glute kickback held for time: on all fours with one leg extended back at hip height, the pelvis level and the glute holding the leg in place.
steps: Start on all fours with the hands under the shoulders and the knees under the hips.
Brace the trunk and keep the pelvis level; do not let the working side rotate upwards.
Extend one leg back and up until the thigh is in line with the torso.
Hold that position for the prescribed time, keeping the neck long and the lower back flat.
Lower the leg under control and repeat on the other side.
tips: Squeeze the glute rather than kicking higher; the height is limited by the pelvis staying square.
Keep the supporting shoulder pushed away from the ear so the upper body does not sag.
A bent knee keeps the tension on the glute, a straight leg shifts more of it to the hamstring.

name: Goblet Squat
desc: A beginner-friendly squat with a kettlebell held at chest height for improved posture and depth.
steps: Hold a kettlebell at chest height with both hands.
Squat down keeping the weight close to your chest.
Drive back up.
Repeat.
tips: The goblet position naturally encourages an upright torso.
Push knees out at the bottom.

name: Good Morning
desc: A hip-hinge movement with a barbell on the back for posterior chain development.
steps: Stand with a barbell across your upper back.
Hinge at the hips, pushing them back while keeping your back flat.
Lower your torso until it's nearly parallel to the floor.
Drive your hips forward to return to standing.
Repeat.
tips: Start with a light bar and master the hinge first.
Keep a soft bend in your knees throughout.
Stop the descent if your lower back starts to round.

name: Hack Squat Calf Raise
desc: A calf raise performed in the hack squat machine, loading the calves heavily without balancing a bar.
steps: Load yourself into a hack squat machine with shoulders under the pads.
Place the balls of your feet on the platform with heels hanging off.
Keep your legs straight with a slight knee bend.
Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels.
Lower your heels back below the platform for a stretch.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Rise as high onto the balls of your feet as possible.
Pause in the bottom stretch instead of bouncing out of it.
Keep your knees straight but not locked to keep tension on the calves.

name: Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Rock
desc: The dynamic version of the kneeling hip-flexor stretch: from a half-kneeling stance the hips rock forward into the stretch and back out of it, repeated instead of held.
steps: Kneel on one knee with the other foot flat on the floor in front of you.
Tuck the tailbone slightly and brace the trunk so the lower back stays neutral.
Rock the hips forward until you feel the front of the back thigh lengthen.
Rock back out of the position under control and repeat rhythmically.
Switch sides and repeat for the same number of repetitions.
tips: Keep the movement in the hips; if the lower back arches, shorten the range.
Squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg during the forward rock.
Pad the down knee with a folded mat if the floor is hard.

name: Half Moon Pose
desc: A standing side balance on one leg and one hand, with the top leg lifted to hip height and the chest turned open towards the ceiling.
steps: From a wide standing stance, bend the front knee and place the bottom hand on the floor or a block ahead of the front foot.
Shift the weight forward and lift the back leg until it is parallel to the floor.
Straighten the standing leg and stack the top hip over the bottom one, reaching the top arm to the ceiling.
Hold the balance for the prescribed time with the lifted foot flexed.
Lower the back foot down and repeat on the other side.
tips: Use a block under the bottom hand; reaching the floor is not the point of the pose.
Press the lifted heel towards the wall behind you to keep the leg switched on.
Look at the floor instead of up if the balance keeps breaking.

name: Handstand Hold
desc: A freestanding static hold balanced upside down on the hands with the body stacked in a straight line. It builds shoulder strength, wrist and trunk stability and balance.
steps: Place the hands about shoulder-width apart on the floor and kick up into an inverted position, one leg after the other.
Press tall through the shoulders and keep the arms locked.
Squeeze the glutes and abdominals so the body forms one straight line from the hands to the toes.
Keep the gaze between the hands and hold the position, making small corrections with the fingers.
Come down under control, one leg at a time, or step out of the hold.
tips: Practise against a wall until you can hold the line without leaning on it.
Push the floor away so the shoulders stay elevated, and pull the ribs in to avoid arching the back.
Warm up the wrists before holding.

name: Handstand Push Ups
desc: An inverted press against a wall, lowering the head to the floor and pressing back up to a full handstand.
steps: Kick up into a handstand against a wall with hands shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core and keep your body straight.
Lower your head toward the floor by bending your elbows.
Stop just before your head touches the ground.
Press through your hands to return to full handstand.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Keep your elbows at roughly 45 degrees rather than flared wide.
Brace your core so your back does not arch away from the wall.
Build up through pike push-ups and partial ranges first.

name: Hang Clean
desc: A clean variation starting with the barbell at the thighs, training explosive triple extension and a fast catch.
steps: Stand holding a barbell with a shoulder-width grip at your thighs.
Hinge at the hips to lower the bar just above your knees.
Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles.
Shrug your shoulders and pull the bar up.
Catch the bar on your front shoulders in a quarter squat.
Stand tall, then return to the hang position.
tips: Hinge to just above the knees before exploding upward.
Shrug and pull the bar up close to your body.
Catch the bar on your shoulders in a quarter squat.

name: Hang Power Clean
desc: A clean from the hang caught in a partial squat, building explosive power without dropping into a full squat.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a barbell at your thighs.
Hinge at the hips to lower the bar to just above the knees.
Drive through your hips and legs explosively.
Pull the bar up and catch it on your front shoulders in a partial squat.
Stand tall with the bar racked on your shoulders.
Lower the bar back to the hang position.
tips: Drive through your hips and legs before the arms pull.
Receive the bar with your thighs above parallel.
Keep your back flat as you hinge to the start position.

name: Hang Snatch
desc: An Olympic lift in which a barbell is pulled from the hang position, just above the knees, to overhead in one explosive movement and caught in a squat. It builds power through the hips, back and shoulders.
steps: Stand with a wide snatch grip on a barbell held at the thighs and the feet about hip-width apart.
Hinge at the hips to lower the bar to just above the knees, keeping the back flat and the shoulders over the bar.
Explosively extend the hips, knees and ankles, shrugging as the bar rises.
Pull yourself under the bar and catch it overhead with locked arms in a squat.
Stand up fully with the bar overhead and stable.
Lower the bar under control back to the thighs and reset.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
Finish the pull with full extension before dropping under the bar.
Learn the movement with a light bar or a dowel; the wide overhead catch needs good shoulder and hip mobility.

name: Hanging Knee Raise
desc: A hanging core exercise on a pull-up bar that targets the lower abs and hip flexors with bent knees.
steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, arms fully extended.
Engage your core and raise your knees toward your chest.
Hold briefly at the top.
Lower your legs slowly back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired reps.
tips: Avoid swinging — initiate the movement from your core.
Exhale as you raise your knees.
Progress to straight-leg raises when this feels easy.

name: Hanging L-Sit
desc: A static core hold hanging from a bar with the legs extended straight in front of the body at hip height, forming an L shape. It demands strong abdominals, hip flexors and grip.
steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, arms straight and the shoulders pulled down.
Brace the abdominals and lift the straight legs until they are parallel to the floor.
Keep the knees locked and the toes pointed, with the legs together.
Hold the position without swinging, breathing steadily.
Lower the legs under control to a dead hang.
tips: If the legs drop below parallel, bend the knees (a tuck hold) and build up from there.
Keep the shoulders active; do not hang passively from the joints.
Squeeze the legs together and point the toes to keep the line tight.

name: Hanging Pike
desc: A strict hanging leg raise taken to the bar — legs stay straight and the feet rise all the way to the hands.
steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip.
Engage the lats and brace the core to create a hollow body.
Keeping the legs perfectly straight, lift them in a smooth arc up to the bar.
Aim to touch the toes to the bar between the hands.
Lower the legs slowly back to the hanging position and repeat.
tips: No swinging — every rep starts from a dead hang with a braced trunk.
If full range is too hard, raise only to horizontal and build up.

name: Hanging Tuck Hold
desc: A static core hold hanging from a bar with the knees pulled up toward the chest. It trains the abdominals and hip flexors and is a step toward the hanging L-sit.
steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip and the arms straight.
Brace the abdominals and pull the knees up toward the chest, rounding the lower back slightly.
Keep the knees together and the thighs at or above hip height.
Hold the tucked position without swinging and breathe steadily.
Lower the legs under control to a full hang.
tips: Curl the pelvis up rather than just lifting the knees; the abdominals should do the work.
Keep the shoulders pulled away from the ears.
End the set when the knees start to drop or the body starts to swing.

name: Happy Baby Pose
desc: A supine hip opener in which the knees are drawn towards the armpits and the feet are held from the outside, releasing the inner thighs and lower back.
steps: Lie on your back and draw both knees towards the chest.
Take hold of the outside edges of the feet, or the shins if the feet are out of reach.
Open the knees wider than the ribs and stack the ankles above the knees, soles facing up.
Press the feet gently into the hands and hold for the prescribed time with the lower back on the floor.
Release the feet and lower the legs.
tips: Keep the tailbone heavy on the floor rather than rolling onto the upper back.
Hold the shins or use a strap around the feet if the grip forces the shoulders off the mat.
Rock gently side to side to massage the lower back if it feels tight.

name: Head-to-Knee Pose
desc: A seated one-legged fold: one leg stays straight while the other foot rests against the inner thigh, so the hamstring of the straight leg lengthens one side at a time.
steps: Sit with one leg straight in front of you and the other knee bent out to the side, that foot at the inner thigh.
Turn the chest towards the straight leg so the navel lines up with the thigh.
Hinge from the hips and reach forward along the straight leg with a long spine.
Hold the fold for the prescribed time, breathing into the back of the leg.
Come up with a flat back and repeat on the other side.
tips: Sit on a folded blanket so the pelvis can tip forward instead of the back rounding.
Keep the toes of the straight leg pointing up rather than rolling out.
Use a strap around the foot when the hands do not reach it comfortably.

name: Heel-Elevated Squat
desc: A squat variation with heels raised on plates or a wedge to shift emphasis onto the quadriceps and improve depth.
steps: Place weight plates or a wedge under your heels, feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a barbell across your upper back or hold dumbbells at your sides.
Brace your core and descend into a squat, keeping your torso upright.
Squat until thighs are parallel to the floor or lower.
Drive through your feet to return to the starting position.
tips: The elevated heels allow a more upright torso and greater knee travel.
Keep your knees tracking over your toes throughout.
Start with a small heel elevation and increase as mobility improves.

name: Heel Flicks
desc: A running warm-up drill that alternates the heels towards the glutes, raising the cadence while dynamically flexing the knees and preparing the hamstrings.
steps: Stand tall with the feet under the hips and the arms bent as for running.
Begin jogging lightly in place.
Flick one heel up towards the same-side glute without driving the knee forward.
Switch feet quickly and continue alternating at an even rhythm.
Stay light on the forefeet and keep the torso upright for the full interval.
tips: Aim for quick relaxed contacts rather than forcing the heel into the glute.
Keep the knees pointing down instead of lifting them like high knees.
Start slowly and increase cadence only after the rhythm feels smooth.

name: Heel-to-Toe Walk
desc: A balance and coordination drill walked along an imaginary line, placing the heel of each step directly against the toes of the other foot so the base of support narrows to almost nothing.
steps: Pick a straight line on the floor and stand on it with your arms out to your sides at shoulder height.
Step forward and place your heel directly in front of — and touching — the toes of the standing foot.
Shift your weight onto the front foot under control, pausing for a moment before the next step.
Bring the back foot through and place it heel to toe again, staying on the line rather than stepping around it.
Look ahead at a fixed point instead of down at your feet, and use your arms to correct any wobble.
Walk the desired number of steps, then turn around and walk back.
tips: Go slowly. Rushing turns it into ordinary walking on a narrow line and removes the balance demand entirely.
If you cannot hold the line, walk beside a wall and touch it only when you need it — that is a regression, not a failure.
Make it harder by folding your arms across your chest, and harder again by doing it with your eyes closed near a wall.

name: Heel Touches
desc: A lying core exercise in which you crunch slightly to one side and reach the hand toward the heel, then alternate sides. It trains the obliques and the upper abdominals with the lower back kept on the floor.
steps: Lie on your back with the knees bent and the feet flat on the floor, about hip-width apart.
Lift the head and shoulders slightly off the floor and reach the arms down along your sides.
Crunch to one side and reach that hand toward the heel on the same side.
Return to the center and reach toward the opposite heel.
Keep alternating sides in a smooth rhythm while the lower back stays on the floor.
Continue for the desired number of repetitions.
tips: Keep the neck long and the chin off the chest; lead with the ribcage, not the head.
Keep each reach small and controlled; the shoulder blades only just clear the floor.
Keep the feet planted and the lower back pressed into the floor throughout.

name: Hero Pose
desc: A kneeling seat with the hips settling between the heels, which lengthens the quadriceps and the front of the ankles while the spine stays tall.
steps: Kneel with the knees together and the feet slightly wider than the hips, tops of the feet flat.
Sit the hips back and down between the heels, using a block or cushion if the floor is out of reach.
Stack the ribs over the pelvis and rest the hands on the thighs.
Hold the seat for the prescribed time, keeping the weight even on both sit bones.
Come out by pressing into the hands and straightening one leg at a time.
tips: Sit on a block whenever the knees complain; the height is a normal part of the pose.
Roll a towel under the ankles if the front of them feels strained.
Keep the feet pointing straight back rather than flaring out to the sides.

name: Hex Bar Deadlift
desc: A deadlift standing inside a hex (trap) bar, keeping the load centered for a more upright, back-friendly pull.
steps: Stand inside a loaded trap bar with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hinge at the hips and knees to grip the handles.
Brace your core and set your back flat.
Drive through your heels and extend hips and knees to stand up.
Lock out at the top with shoulders pulled back.
Lower the bar back to the floor under control.
tips: Keep your chest up and back flat as you set your grip.
Push the floor away rather than yanking the bar with your back.
Stand fully upright at the top without leaning back.

name: High-Foot Leg Press
desc: A leg press with the feet placed high on the platform, shifting more of the movement toward hip extension and the gluteus maximus while the back stays supported.
steps: Set the back pad and seat so your lower back stays supported and your knees can bend without your pelvis rolling under.
Place both feet high on the platform at about shoulder width, with the toes tracking in the same direction as the knees.
Lower the sled by bending the hips and knees until you reach a comfortable depth without the lower back lifting from the pad.
Press through the whole foot and extend the hips and knees without locking the knees aggressively.
Lower the sled under control and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
tips: Keep the pelvis heavy against the pad; a high foot position does not justify rounding the lower back at the bottom.
Keep the heels and the whole foot planted rather than letting the toes carry the sled.
Use a depth that preserves pelvic position instead of chasing a deeper range with a tucked pelvis.

name: High Knees
desc: A bodyweight cardio drill where the knees are driven up to hip height in rapid alternation.
steps: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Drive one knee up toward the chest while pumping the opposite arm.
Quickly switch legs, mirroring the arm action.
Continue alternating at a fast pace.
Continue for the prescribed work interval.
tips: Drive the knees up to at least hip height.
Stay light on the balls of the feet.
Keep the torso upright — do not lean back.

name: High Plank
desc: A plank variation with arms fully extended in a push-up position.
steps: Start in a push-up position with arms fully extended.
Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and hold the position.
Breathe steadily throughout.
tips: Stack your shoulders directly above your wrists.
Squeeze your glutes to keep your hips from sagging.
Push the floor away to avoid sinking between your shoulder blades.

name: Machine Hip Abduction
desc: A machine exercise targeting the outer hip muscles.
steps: Sit in the hip abduction machine with pads against your outer thighs.
Push your legs apart against the resistance.
Hold briefly at the widest point.
Return to the starting position with control.
Repeat.
tips: Sit tall and keep your back against the pad.
Don't let the weight stack slam down between reps.
Choose a resistance that allows a full range of motion.

name: Hip Adduction
desc: A machine exercise pressing the legs together against resistance, isolating and strengthening the inner-thigh adductors.
steps: Sit on the hip adduction machine with your back against the pad.
Place your legs against the pads with the machine set to a comfortable stretch.
Squeeze your legs together until the pads meet in the middle.
Hold the squeeze briefly in the fully closed position.
Let your legs open back out under control to the start.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Choose a start width that stretches without straining your groin.
Move through the whole range at an even, controlled speed.
Do not let the weight stack slam down as your legs open back out.

name: Hollow Body Hold
desc: An isometric core hold borrowed from gymnastics, training total-body tension with the spine in a slight C-shape.
steps: Lie on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Press the lower back firmly into the floor.
Lift the shoulders, head, and legs slightly off the floor.
Hold the position with arms and legs extended, body in a shallow banana shape.
Hold for the prescribed time.
tips: Keep the lower back glued to the floor — if it lifts, raise the legs higher.
Tuck the chin slightly to engage the upper abs.
Bend the knees to scale if the position breaks.

name: Horizontal Leg Press
desc: A machine leg press performed horizontally, targeting quads, glutes, and hamstrings.
steps: Sit in a horizontal leg press machine and place feet shoulder-width apart.
Unlock the machine and lower the platform toward your chest.
Press the platform back to the start.
Repeat.
tips: Do not let your lower back lift off the seat.
Avoid locking out the knees completely.

name: Human Flag
desc: An advanced calisthenics isometric hold with the body horizontal on a vertical pole, parallel to the ground.
steps: Stand close to a sturdy vertical pole.
Grip the pole high with the top hand (overhand) and lower with the bottom hand (underhand).
Kick the legs up and out while pressing the bottom arm hard against the pole.
Extend the body horizontally so it forms a straight line parallel to the ground.
Hold the position with the body rigid for the target time.
Lower under control.
tips: Build up to the full flag with tucked and straddle progressions first.
The bottom arm pushes; the top arm pulls — they balance the lever.
Engage the lats, obliques, and glutes hard to stay rigid.

name: Hyperextension Bench Hold
desc: An isometric hold on a hyperextension bench: you lift your torso until your body forms one straight line from the heels to the head and hold it there. The erector spinae and the glutes stay under tension without the swinging of the dynamic back extension.
steps: Adjust the bench so that the pad sits just below your hip bones and your heels are hooked firmly behind the roller or pad.
Cross your arms over your chest and lower your torso toward the floor with a straight back.
Raise your torso until your body is in one straight line from your head to your heels.
Stop in that line and hold, with your glutes squeezed and your neck in line with your spine.
Keep your breathing slow and do not arch your lower back past the straight line while you hold for the planned time.
Lower your torso under control and rest.
tips: Stop at a straight line; leaning back past it hands the work to your lower back joints instead of the muscles.
Squeeze the glutes during the whole hold, so that the hips stay extended and the lower back is not doing the job alone.
Hold a weight plate against your chest only after you can hold bodyweight for a full minute.

name: Inchworm
desc: A bodyweight warm-up and mobility drill: from a standing forward fold you walk your hands out along the floor until your body is in a low plank, with the elbows bent as at the bottom of a push-up, then walk them back toward your feet. It stretches the hamstrings and calves while the shoulders, chest and trunk hold the low plank.
steps: Stand tall with your feet about hip-width apart.
Hinge forward at the hips and place your hands on the floor in front of your feet, bending the knees slightly if you need to.
Walk your hands forward one at a time, keeping your legs as straight as you comfortably can, until your body is in a straight line close to the floor.
Bend your elbows so your chest hovers just above the floor, as at the bottom of a push-up, and pause briefly with your trunk braced.
Walk your hands back toward your feet in small steps, raising your hips, until you are back in the forward fold.
Stand up, or go straight into the next repetition.
tips: Keep the knees as straight as you can so the hamstrings and calves get the stretch; a slight bend is fine if your hands do not reach the floor.
Brace the trunk in the low plank so the hips do not sag or pike up. For an easier version, stop in a straight-arm plank and skip the lowering.
Take small, controlled steps; walking out too far, too fast makes you collapse onto the floor.

name: Incline EZ-Bar Bench Press
desc: An incline press with an EZ-bar targeting the upper chest with a joint-friendly grip.
steps: Set bench to 30–45 degrees. Grip the EZ-bar with hands on the angled sections.
Lower the bar to your upper chest.
Press back up to full extension.
Repeat.
tips: The incline shifts emphasis to the upper pectorals.
Control the descent to avoid shoulder strain.

name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
desc: A bicep curl on an incline bench for a deeper stretch of the long head.
steps: Sit on an incline bench set to 45 degrees, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Let your arms hang straight down with palms forward.
Curl the dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
Lower with control to full extension.
Repeat.
tips: Keep your head and shoulders against the bench throughout.
Don't let your elbows drift forward as you curl.
Avoid shrugging your shoulders forward as you lift the weight.

name: Incline Dumbbell Fly
desc: An incline isolation exercise opening dumbbells in a wide arc, stretching and targeting the upper chest.
steps: Lie back on an incline bench holding dumbbells above your chest.
Press the dumbbells up with palms facing each other.
Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Lower the dumbbells in a wide arc until you feel a chest stretch.
Squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbells back together.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Keep a fixed slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Lower only as far as a comfortable chest stretch allows.
Squeeze your chest to bring the dumbbells back together.

name: Incline Hammer Curl
desc: A hammer curl performed on an incline bench for increased stretch and biceps long-head activation.
steps: Sit on an incline bench holding dumbbells with a neutral grip.
Allow arms to hang straight.
Curl the dumbbells up in a hammer motion.
Lower slowly.
Repeat.
tips: The incline provides a greater stretch.
Avoid swinging.

name: Incline Plank Hold
desc: An easier version of the plank: with your forearms resting on a flat bench and your feet on the floor, you hold your body in a straight line from head to heels. The raised hands reduce the load on the shoulders and make it a good starting point for the full plank.
steps: Place your forearms on a flat bench, with your elbows directly under your shoulders.
Step your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
Squeeze your glutes and pull your belly button toward your spine to keep your hips level.
Keep your neck long and look at a point on the bench slightly ahead of your hands.
Hold the position for the planned time while breathing steadily.
Step your feet in to finish.
tips: Do not let your hips sag toward the bench or pike up; your body should stay in one straight line.
Press your forearms into the bench and push the bench away to keep your shoulder blades wide.
Step your feet further back to make it harder, or closer to make it easier; make sure the bench cannot slide.

name: Incline Push-Up
desc: A beginner-friendly push-up variation with hands elevated on a bench or step.
steps: Place your hands on a bench or elevated surface, shoulder-width apart.
Extend your legs behind you into a plank position.
Lower your chest toward the bench by bending your elbows.
Push back up to the starting position.
Repeat.
tips: Check that the elevated surface is stable before starting.
Keep your elbows tucked rather than flared out wide.
Progress to a lower surface as you get stronger.

name: Inverted Row
desc: A horizontal bodyweight pulling exercise performed under a fixed bar, pulling the chest to the bar while keeping the body rigid.
steps: Set a barbell in a rack at about waist height.
Lie underneath and grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip.
Hang with arms extended, heels on the floor, body straight from head to ankles.
Pull your chest to the bar, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Lower yourself under control until arms are fully extended.
Repeat.
tips: Keep the core braced — no hip sag.
To make it harder, elevate your feet; to make it easier, walk your feet in toward the bar.
Pause briefly at the top with the chest against the bar.

name: Isometric Neck Lateral Flexion
desc: A static side-neck drill using the hand as resistance against the head, training the sternocleidomastoid and scalene without hardware.
steps: Sit or stand tall. Place the palm of one hand against the side of the head, above the ear.
Press the head into the hand while resisting equally with the hand — the head does not move.
Hold the isometric contraction for 5 to 10 seconds.
Release slowly, then repeat on the same side for the set.
Switch sides and repeat.
tips: Match the pressure; this is 50% effort, not a wrestling match.
Keep the jaw relaxed and the shoulders down.

name: Isometric Split Squat
desc: A held version of the split squat: you stand in a long lunge stance and stay in the bottom position with your front thigh near parallel to the floor. The continuous tension builds strength and control in the quadriceps and glutes of the front leg.
steps: Stand with one foot well forward and the other foot back, about a long stride apart, with your hands on your hips.
Keep your torso upright and lower straight down by bending both knees.
Lower until your front thigh is close to parallel with the floor and your back knee hovers just above the ground.
Keep your front heel flat and your front knee tracking over your toes.
Hold this position for the planned time, keeping your trunk tall and your weight spread through the front foot.
Press up to the top, then repeat on the other leg.
tips: Keep the back knee just off the floor so the front leg keeps working the whole time.
Do not let the front knee cave inward; push it gently over the middle toes.
Hold a lighter position higher up if the bottom is too intense; the quads should burn, not the knee joint.

name: Jackknife Sit-Up
desc: A full-body crunch performed lying on the floor, lifting both legs and torso simultaneously to touch hands to feet.
steps: Lie face-up on the floor with arms extended overhead and legs extended straight.
Simultaneously lift the torso and the straight legs off the floor.
Reach the hands up toward the feet as the feet rise — meet above the hips.
Lower the torso and legs back to the floor under control.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: Arms and legs move at the same speed — avoid a kick-first cheat.
If the lower back arches on the return, slow down and don't fully touch the floor.

name: Jefferson Curl
desc: A loaded spinal-flexion drill: standing tall with a light weight, you round the spine one vertebra at a time and restack it, building segmental control and hamstring/spinal-erector flexibility under load.
steps: Stand tall holding a light dumbbell with straight arms, feet roughly hip-width.
Tuck your chin and begin rounding the spine from the top, one vertebra at a time.
Curl down slowly, letting the weight hang and keeping the legs mostly straight.
Reach the bottom with the back fully rounded and a stretch through the hamstrings.
Reverse it, restacking the spine from the bottom up back to standing.
tips: Use a very light weight -- this is a controlled mobility drill, not a heavy lift.
Round segment by segment; do not hinge at the hips like a stiff-leg deadlift.
Move slowly and never bounce at the bottom.

name: Jump Rope
desc: A classic cardio drill that trains calves, ankles, and timing with a rope and rhythmic hops.
steps: Hold a jump rope handle in each hand with the rope behind you.
Swing the rope overhead and forward in a smooth arc.
Hop just high enough for the rope to pass under your feet.
Land softly on the balls of the feet, knees slightly bent.
Keep a steady rhythm for the prescribed interval.
tips: Use the wrists to spin the rope, not the shoulders.
Hop low — only an inch or two off the floor.
Stay tall with elbows close to the sides.

name: Jump Squat
desc: A plyometric bodyweight squat where you explode upward into a vertical jump.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Drop into a quarter-squat with the arms back.
Explode upward, swinging the arms up and jumping as high as you can.
Land softly back into a quarter-squat to absorb impact.
Repeat without pausing for the prescribed reps.
tips: Land softly with bent knees to absorb impact.
Drive the arms up to add height to the jump.
Keep the chest up — do not let the torso collapse.

name: Jumping Jacks
desc: This classic full-body dynamic exercise elevates heart rate and targets the calves, shoulders, quads, and glutes, making it an excellent warm-up or conditioning movement.
steps: Stand tall with feet together and arms at your sides.
Simultaneously jump your feet out wide and raise your arms overhead.
Ensure your arms meet or nearly meet above your head.
Jump your feet back together while lowering your arms to your sides.
Maintain a continuous, rhythmic motion.
tips: Land softly on the balls of your feet to absorb impact.
Keep your core engaged throughout the movement.
Control your breathing; inhale as you jump out, exhale as you jump in.
Increase speed for a greater cardiovascular challenge.

name: Kettlebell Step-Up to Balance
desc: A loaded version of the step-up to balance: holding a kettlebell in each hand, you step onto a low platform, drive the free knee up in front of you and stand tall on the working leg before stepping back down. The quadriceps and glutes lift the body and the weights while the hips and ankle keep you steady.
steps: Stand facing a low, stable step or bench with a kettlebell in each hand, arms hanging at your sides.
Place one foot flat on top of the step.
Press through the whole of the front foot and straighten that leg to lift your body onto the step.
As you rise, drive the other knee up in front of you until the thigh is about hip height.
Stand tall on the working leg and hold the knee-up position for a moment without leaning back.
Lower the free foot back to the floor under control, then step the working leg down as well and repeat; switch legs after the planned repetitions.
tips: Keep the weights hanging at your sides and still; swinging them or pulling them up with your arms takes the work away from the legs.
Keep your trunk upright and your hips level during the balance hold rather than tilting toward the lifted knee.
Start with light weights and a low step; add load only when you can hold the balance position without wobbling.

name: Kettlebell Bottoms-Up Hold
desc: A one-arm hold in which the kettlebell is held upside down by the handle at shoulder height, with the bell above your hand. Keeping the bell level demands a very firm grip and constant work from the forearm and the shoulder, which makes this a strong test of wrist and shoulder stability.
steps: Clean a kettlebell to your shoulder and flip it so that the bell points up and the handle sits in your fist.
Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and your free arm relaxed at your side.
Keep your forearm vertical and your elbow close to your ribs, with the bell directly above your hand.
Grip the handle firmly and keep your wrist straight, as if you were balancing a cup.
Hold the bell steady for the planned time, breathing slowly and keeping your shoulder down.
Lower the kettlebell with control, turn it the right way up and switch arms.
tips: Start with a very light bell; a weight that feels easy when held the normal way can be hard to keep level.
Keep the shoulder down and the wrist stacked over the forearm; if the bell tips, reset the position before it falls.
Stand in a clear space, away from people and furniture, in case the bell tips.

name: Kettlebell Bulgarian Split Squat
desc: This unilateral squat variation builds lower body strength, muscle, and stability by elevating the rear foot and holding a kettlebell, primarily targeting the quadriceps and glutes.
steps: Stand facing away from a bench, placing one foot on it behind you, laces down. Hold a kettlebell in the hand opposite your front leg.
Maintain an upright torso and engage your core.
Lower your body by bending both knees, allowing your front knee to track over your toes.
Descend until your front thigh is parallel to the floor or slightly below, keeping your rear knee close to the ground.
Drive through your front heel to return to the starting position, extending your hips and knees.
Complete all reps per side before switching.
tips: Ensure your front foot is far enough from the bench to allow a full range of motion without discomfort.
Keep your torso upright throughout the movement to maximize glute and quad engagement.
Control the eccentric (lowering) phase to build strength and stability.
Experiment with holding the kettlebell in the same hand as the working leg (ipsilateral) or the opposite hand (contralateral) for different challenges.

name: Kettlebell Close-Grip Floor Press
desc: A floor press performed with a single kettlebell gripped close together with both hands. The narrow grip and the floor stop on the elbows shift emphasis off the chest and onto the triceps, with no shoulder hyperextension.
steps: Lie on your back on the floor with the knees bent and feet flat.
Hold a single kettlebell by the handle with both hands, close together, the bell resting on the chest with elbows tucked tight to the ribs.
Brace the core and press the kettlebell straight up until the arms are fully extended.
Lower under control until the upper arms touch the floor and pause briefly.
Press back up to lockout.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked at roughly 30–45 degrees from the torso — wide elbows turn it into a chest press.
The brief pause when the elbows touch the floor kills the bounce and forces a clean concentric.
Pick a bell you can control with two hands; the narrow grip is unforgiving if it tips.

name: Kettlebell Concentration Curl
desc: A seated single-arm bicep isolation move: the elbow braces against the inner thigh while curling a kettlebell, keeping the upper arm still so the bicep does all the work.
steps: Sit on a bench with your feet wide, holding a kettlebell in one hand.
Brace the back of your upper arm against the inside of your thigh, letting the kettlebell hang.
Curl the kettlebell up toward your shoulder, keeping the elbow pinned against your leg.
Squeeze the bicep at the top, then lower slowly under control.
Finish all reps on one side, then switch arms.
tips: Keep the upper arm braced and still -- only the forearm moves.
Rotate the wrist slightly as you curl for a stronger peak contraction.
Use a lighter weight than a standard curl -- strict form matters more here.

name: Kettlebell Curl
desc: A biceps curl with one kettlebell held by the handle in both hands. The kettlebell hangs in front of your thighs and you curl it up toward your chest, keeping the elbows close to your sides; sharing the load between two hands makes it an easy way to start training the biceps.
steps: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and hold the kettlebell by its handle with both hands, so it hangs in front of your thighs.
Keep your elbows close to your sides, your chest tall and your shoulders relaxed.
Bend your elbows and curl the kettlebell up toward your chest without letting your upper arms swing forward.
Squeeze your biceps at the top, with the kettlebell close to your chest.
Lower the kettlebell slowly until your arms are straight again, keeping control of the swing of the bell.
Repeat for the planned repetitions.
tips: Hold the handle firmly with both hands and keep your wrists straight, so the kettlebell does not roll or tilt.
Do not lean back or swing your hips to lift the kettlebell; if you have to, the weight is too heavy.
Take about twice as long to lower the kettlebell as to lift it, so the biceps work through the whole descent.

name: Kettlebell Curl Iso Hold
desc: An isometric version of the kettlebell curl: you curl a kettlebell held by the handle in both hands until your forearms are level with the floor and hold it there. The biceps and the brachialis stay under constant tension at the point where the lift is hardest.
steps: Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart and hold the kettlebell by its handle with both hands, so it hangs in front of your thighs.
Keep your elbows close to your sides and your shoulders relaxed.
Curl the kettlebell up until your forearms are level with the floor and the elbows are bent to about 90 degrees.
Stop there and hold the kettlebell steady, hanging in front of your body.
Keep your upper arms still, your chest tall and your breathing slow while you hold for the planned time.
Lower the kettlebell under control and rest.
tips: Keep the kettlebell steady; swaying or letting it drop toward your thighs takes the load off the biceps.
Do not lean back to hold the weight; your trunk stays upright and your elbows stay close to your sides.
Choose a lighter kettlebell than for the curl itself, since the hold is hard at the halfway point.

name: Kettlebell Deadlift
desc: A foundational hip-hinge pull lifting a kettlebell from the floor, training the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and kettlebell between your feet.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to grip the handle.
Brace your core and set your back flat.
Drive through your heels to stand up with the kettlebell.
Lock out at the top with shoulders pulled back.
Lower the kettlebell back to the floor with control.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to your shins as you lift.
Think of pushing the floor away rather than lifting with your back.
Look at a spot on the floor ahead to keep your neck neutral.

name: Kettlebell Farmer's Walk
desc: A loaded carry with heavy kettlebells at the sides, building grip strength and full-body stability.
steps: Stand between two heavy kettlebells.
Hinge and grip the handles firmly with a neutral grip.
Stand tall with shoulders back and core braced.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps.
Maintain an upright posture throughout the walk.
Set the weights down at the end of the distance.
tips: Keep your shoulders level and avoid leaning to either side.
Breathe steadily rather than holding your breath under load.
If your grip fails, set the weights down away from your feet.

name: Kettlebell Floor Press
desc: A two-arm chest press performed lying on the floor with a kettlebell in each hand. The floor caps the ROM (triceps hit the floor before full stretch), making it shoulder-friendly and a great home option.
steps: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent, feet flat.
Hold a kettlebell in each hand at the chest, bells resting on the outer forearms.
Press both kettlebells straight up until the arms are fully extended.
Lower under control until the triceps touch the floor — do not bounce.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions.
tips: Elbows stay about 45 degrees from the torso; do not flare.
The grip matters: keep the bells stable against the outside of the forearms.
The floor limits ROM by design — this is the feature, not the bug.

name: Kettlebell Goblet Lunge
desc: This unilateral compound exercise strengthens the quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings by performing a lunge while holding a kettlebell in the goblet position, improving lower body strength and stability.
steps: Stand tall holding a kettlebell by its horns at chest height, elbows tucked, in the goblet position.
Take a controlled step forward with one leg, lowering your hips until both knees are bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Ensure your front knee is stacked over your ankle and your rear knee hovers just above the floor.
Drive through your front heel to return to the starting position, maintaining balance and core tension.
Complete all repetitions on one side before switching, or alternate legs per set.
tips: Keep your chest upright and core braced throughout the movement to protect your spine and maintain stability.
Focus on a controlled descent and a powerful drive up, engaging your glutes and quads.
Avoid letting your front knee collapse inward; keep it aligned with your toes.

name: Kettlebell Halo
desc: A shoulder-mobility drill where a kettlebell is circled around the head. Warms up the rotator cuff, thoracic spine, and shoulder girdle with minimal load.
steps: Stand tall, core braced, holding a light kettlebell by the horns (upside down) at chest height.
Raise the bell to one side of your head and pass it around the back in a smooth circle.
Bring it back to the starting position in front of your face.
Reverse direction every few reps.
Repeat for the recommended number of repetitions or time.
tips: Light weight only — this is mobility, not strength.
Keep the head stationary; the bell goes around, not the head.
If the bell drifts wide, shrink the circle — tight orbit, close to the skull.

name: Kettlebell Hammer Curl
desc: A neutral-grip curl gripping the handle of a kettlebell so that the bell hangs alongside the wrist. The offset mass and neutral grip bias the brachialis and brachioradialis.
steps: Stand holding a kettlebell in one hand, gripping the handle in a neutral position (palm facing the body).
The bell rests on or beside the forearm.
Keep the elbow tucked to the side and curl the bell up toward the shoulder.
Squeeze at the top, then lower under control.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
tips: Control the offset mass — the bell wants to rotate at the bottom of the ROM.
Elbow stays still; only the forearm moves.
Light load — this biases brachialis, not peak bicep size.

name: Kettlebell Hip Thrust
desc: This exercise effectively targets the gluteus maximus and hamstrings, using a kettlebell to add resistance for powerful hip extension and glute development.
steps: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench, knees bent, and feet flat.
Place a kettlebell across your hips, holding it securely with both hands.
Drive through your heels, lifting your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Squeeze your glutes forcefully at the top of the movement.
Slowly lower your hips back down to the starting position with control.
tips: Keep your chin tucked towards your chest to maintain a neutral spine.
Focus on pushing through your heels to maximize glute activation.
Ensure your knees track in line with your toes throughout the movement.
Control the eccentric phase, resisting the weight as you lower your hips.

name: Kettlebell Kickstand Deadlift
desc: A staggered-stance hip hinge with one kettlebell that loads the front leg while the back foot lightly stabilizes.
steps: Stand tall and step one foot back so only the toes touch the floor.
Hold a kettlebell in one hand at hip height.
Hinge at the hips, lowering the kettlebell toward mid-shin while keeping the back flat.
Keep most of your weight on the front foot throughout.
Drive through the front heel to return to standing. Switch sides after all reps.
tips: Keep the kettlebell close to the shin on the descent.
Stop at the point of hamstring stretch in the front leg.
Complete all reps on one side before switching.

name: Kettlebell Lunge Press
desc: A combination exercise pressing a kettlebell overhead with one arm while lunging, training legs, shoulders, and core.
steps: Hold a kettlebell at shoulder height with one arm.
Step forward into a lunge with the opposite leg.
As you lunge, press the kettlebell overhead.
Lock out the arm at the top of the press.
Step back to standing while lowering the kettlebell.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
tips: Brace your core to resist leaning toward the loaded side.
Keep your front knee tracking in line with your toes.
Avoid arching your back as you lock out overhead.

name: Kettlebell Offset Reverse Lunge and Press
desc: A reverse lunge with a single kettlebell pressed overhead, the offset load challenging balance and core stability.
steps: Hold a kettlebell at shoulder height on one side.
Step backward into a reverse lunge with the opposite leg.
As you reach the bottom of the lunge, press the kettlebell overhead.
Drive through your front heel to return to standing.
Lower the kettlebell back to shoulder height.
Complete reps on one side, then switch.
tips: Keep your hips square as you step back into the lunge.
Brace your trunk to resist bending toward the loaded side.
Lower your back knee with control instead of dropping into the bottom.

name: Kettlebell Overhead Carry
desc: A loaded walk with a single kettlebell locked out overhead, where the bell hangs behind the wrist and pulls the arm backwards, making it harder to hold still than a dumbbell.
steps: Clean and press a kettlebell to lockout, letting the bell settle on the back of your forearm.
Straighten the elbow fully and turn the arm so the bell sits behind and above your wrist rather than off to the side.
Keep the shoulder active: push the weight up toward the ceiling and let the shoulder blade rotate up with it rather than forcing it down.
Brace your trunk and walk forward with even strides, keeping the bell stacked over your shoulder and hip.
Keep your wrist straight; letting it bend back is what makes an overhead bell feel unstable.
Carry for the desired distance, lower under control, then repeat on the other side.
tips: Go lighter than you would with a dumbbell. The offset mass makes the same weight noticeably harder to keep still.
A bent wrist is the usual failure point. If it keeps collapsing, drop the weight rather than fighting it for the whole distance.
Do both sides for the same distance — the unilateral load is the point of the exercise.

name: Kettlebell Overhead Hold
desc: A one-arm isometric hold with the kettlebell locked out overhead. The shoulder, the upper back and the trunk work together to keep the bell steady over your head, which trains shoulder stability and the finish position of the press.
steps: Clean or press a kettlebell up so that your arm is straight overhead with the bell resting against the back of your forearm.
